title: Actually, Starliner might fly into space this year
gist: Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg says the Starliner propulsion redesign is largely done and the remaining gate is ISS port availability, putting a cargo test flight in play for 2026 and crew in late 2027—just as SpaceX signals it will retire Crew Dragon by 2030, setting up a structurally more expensive decade for human access to low-Earth orbit.

insights.claim: Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told analysts on the quarterly earnings call that the redesign of Starliner's deficiencies is going quite well, a notably more confident posture than NASA's February position.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: CEO-level confidence on an earnings call is the strongest public signal yet that Boeing sees the program's technical risk as retired—relevant to further charge-taking.
insights.quote: The redesign of the Starliner deficiencies is going quite well, and we’re feeling pretty good about that,

insights.claim: The binding constraint on Starliner's next launch is no longer engineering but scheduling with NASA for an open ISS docking port and astronaut time to unload cargo, confirmed independently to Ars by an official.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: When the gate shifts from technical to logistical, schedule risk drops sharply—raises the probability of a 2026 flight materially.
insights.locator: During the earnings call Ortberg suggested much of that work was completed

insights.claim: If the cargo test flight goes well and the propulsion modifications hold, a crewed Starliner mission is possible in late 2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A late-2027 crew date means Starliner would have roughly three years of overlap with Crew Dragon before the 2030 retirement—thin, but non-zero, redundancy.
insights.locator: It is therefore possible that Starliner launches this year

insights.claim: NASA formally classified the 2024 crewed Starliner flight as a 'Type A' mishap, the agency's acknowledgement that the test flight was a serious failure that stranded astronauts Butch Wilmore and Sunny Williams until a Crew Dragon returned them in early 2025.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Formal mishap classification is the regulatory baseline against which any return-to-flight optimism must be discounted.
insights.locator: When we last checked in on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft in February

themes.theme: Fixed-price contracting has been ruinous for Boeing

insights.claim: Boeing has taken approximately $2 billion in charges on Starliner due to development delays and the need for additional test flights after software and propulsion failures, all under the fixed-price Commercial Crew contract signed with NASA in 2014.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A $2 billion loss on a fixed-price government contract is the canonical cautionary tale shaping how primes now bid on NASA and DoD programs.
insights.locator: To date Boeing has taken approximately $2 billion in charges

insights.claim: Ortberg indicated further delays would only push Boeing deeper into the red, while stating he does not currently anticipate the NASA scheduling uncertainty creating a cost problem.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Management is explicitly guiding away from another charge—watch subsequent quarters for whether that guidance holds.
insights.quote: I don’t at this time anticipate that’s going to create a cost problem for us, but we do have some uncertainty here that we’ve got to work with NASA to get that put to bed
insights.locator: We’ve got to work with NASA to align on the launches

insights.claim: Starliner's Service Module, which houses all the costly propulsion systems, burns up in the atmosphere rather than returning, and sources put the expendable module's cost at tens of millions of dollars per flight.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A permanent per-flight cost floor tens of millions above a reusable competitor makes Starliner structurally uncompetitive absent a mandated second supplier.
insights.locator: Its Service Module, which houses all of the costly propulsion systems

insights.claim: After its initial run of NASA missions Starliner will have no rocket, because the Atlas V is retiring; ULA's Vulcan is an option but human-rating it carries not-inconsiderable cost and would still be more expensive than Falcon 9.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A capsule without a certified launcher has no commercial future—the human-rating capex is the hidden liability in any Starliner valuation.
insights.locator: There is also the fact that, after its initial run of NASA missions

insights.claim: Boeing began shopping some of its space assets including Starliner a year and a half ago but has closed no sale, with one source attributing the failure to Boeing asking too high a price.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A bid-ask gap on distressed space assets that has persisted 18 months suggests eventual markdown—watch for a lower-priced deal or a write-off.

insights.claim: Blue Origin, the obvious deep-pocketed buyer, chose instead to press on with developing its own in-house crew vehicle rather than acquiring Starliner.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The most capable potential acquirer passing is a strong negative signal on Starliner's standalone economics.
insights.locator: One potential industry partner with deep pockets, Blue Origin

insights.claim: SpaceX has been telling industry officials it plans to retire Crew Dragon no later than 2030 in favor of Starship, creating uncertainty about crew access precisely when NASA may want to fly to the ISS into the early 2030s.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A hard sunset date on the only reliable crew vehicle is the single biggest structural risk to the commercial LEO economy—creates a bid for any credible alternative.

insights.claim: Planned private space stations intended to replace the ISS are already having difficulty negotiating crew transportation services because of the Dragon retirement uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Transport uncertainty is directly impairing the financeability of commercial station ventures—a second-order drag on the whole LEO buildout.
insights.quote: These companies are having difficulties negotiating crew transportation services as a result.
insights.locator: This raises serious concerns for not just NASA

insights.claim: Crew Dragon is by far the preferred option today because it has proven reliable and offers the lowest cost thanks to reusability and flying on Falcon 9.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Establishes the price and reliability benchmark every competitor must clear—and the baseline that disappears in 2030.
insights.locator: Crew Dragon is, for now at least, by far the preferred option

insights.claim: The space community is not yet comfortable launching humans on Starship, so SpaceX's own succession plan carries adoption risk independent of the vehicle's technical readiness.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Certification and cultural acceptance, not just engineering, gate Starship crew flights—extending the window where Starliner has strategic value.
insights.locator: In a world where SpaceX seeks to retire Dragon

insights.claim: The cost of human spaceflight to low-Earth orbit in the 2030s is going to be significantly more expensive than in the 2020s, at least until Starship really takes off.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A rising cost curve inverts the prevailing 'access to space keeps getting cheaper' assumption—reprice any business model dependent on cheap crew transport this decade.
insights.quote: No matter what happens, the cost of human spaceflight into low-Earth orbit during the 2030s is going to be significantly more expensive than the cost in the 2020s
